summary:
Montana stands under the legal framework of the United States and under a state constitution whose equal-protection and dignity guarantees state courts have repeatedly applied to block or enjoin anti-trans legislation. In the July 2026 anti-trans national legal risk assessment, Montana is the only state whose standing improved, on the strength of that court record, even though the statutes that would otherwise place it among the most restrictive states remain enacted.

Senate Bill 458, signed in May 2023, codified sex as an immutable male-female binary determined at birth and unchangeable. District Judge Leslie Halligan struck it down in February 2025, holding that it violated the equal-protection clauses of the Montana Constitution by leaving a gap in sex-discrimination protection. Senate Bill 437, signed 24 March 2026, codified biological definitions of gender, male, female, man, woman, mother and father based on primary sexual anatomy, provides that gender means that sex definition and not gender identity, experienced gender, expression or role, and applies across more than 60 sections of state law including driver's licences, marriage licences and anti-discrimination protections, with applicants for driver's and marriage licences required to list sex as so defined. Representative Zooey Zephyr stated that the bill erases transgender, intersex and Two-Spirit recognition; in April 2026 plaintiffs sought to add it to the ongoing litigation as fundamentally identical to SB 458.

Changes to sex markers on Montana identity documents have been blocked in court since 2022. A rule of 9 September 2022 barring changes to sex identification on birth certificates absent proof of data-entry error or a DNA test was blocked by court order on 15 September 2022, which the Department of Public Health and Human Services complied with. A bill of 22 February 2023 prohibiting gender-marker changes on all identity documents, signed 19 May 2023, was stopped by a December 2024 injunction from District Judge Mike Menahan; after an April 2024 suit by two trans women unable to update driver's licences and birth certificates, Judge Menahan issued a preliminary block on 16 December 2024 pending trial on sex-discrimination grounds, which the Montana Supreme Court upheld on 15 April 2026, holding that the constitution requires treating individuals with dignity. A Helena district court's December 2024 order also enjoined the 2022 health department rule, the Motor Vehicle Division policy requiring a birth certificate to change a driver's-licence sex marker, and portions of SB 458, finding the plaintiffs likely to succeed on the claim that the restrictions constitute sex discrimination under the state constitution.

Facilities access is governed by a statute that is not in force. House Bill 121, passed in February 2025, requires bathrooms, locker rooms and sleeping areas in publicly funded facilities to be segregated by biological sex assigned at birth; the ACLU of Montana sued immediately, and on 2 April 2025 District Judge Shane Vannatta issued a temporary restraint, finding the law motivated by animus and supported by no evidence that the restrictions advance women's safety and privacy. A proposal to forbid trans people from using Capitol bathrooms aligned with their gender was voted down by the Montana House on 3 December 2024, and a 2018 ballot initiative requiring public bathroom use to match birth-certificate gender failed to gather signatures.

Gender-affirming care for minors is not prohibited in Montana. Senate 99, signed 28 April 2023, banned such care and was described as the most comprehensive prohibition in the United States; District Judge Jason Marks preliminarily enjoined it on 27 September 2023, ruling that discrimination against a person for being transgender inherently constitutes sex discrimination under Bostock v. Clayton County and served no compelling governmental interest in protecting minors. The Montana Supreme Court kept the injunction in place on 11 December 2024 on privacy grounds, with Justice Laurie McKinnon adding that transgender status should be treated as a suspect class, and Judge Marks permanently struck the ban down on 14 May 2025 for failure to establish a bona fide health risk clearly and convincingly or to show a change in the stance of major U.S. medical organizations.

A 2021 law barring transgender athletes from public school sports, contingent on continued federal education funding and signed the following month by Governor Greg Gianforte, was struck down in September 2022 by District Judge Rienne McElyea as unconstitutional on administrative grounds for infringing the authority of the Regents of the Montana University System.

Protection against discrimination is thinner than the court record suggests. By executive order Montana prohibits gender-identity discrimination in state employment and by state contractors and subcontractors, originating in 2000 personnel rules, broadened by Executive Order 41-2008 in November 2008 and expanded to gender identity and contractors in January 2016; federal Title VII protection for gender identity under Bostock v. Clayton County applies in Montana, and ordinances in Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish prohibit gender-identity discrimination in public and private employment, housing and public accommodations, with Missoula County covering county employees only. Montana hate-crime statutes do not include gender identity, leaving prosecution to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. In April 2021 Governor Gianforte signed legislation granting a right to discriminate where religious beliefs are substantially burdened, widely viewed as a licence to discriminate against LGBTQ people.

Same-sex marriage has been recognised in Montana since 19 November 2014, when Judge Brian Morris enjoined the state ban effective immediately, a ruling mooted by Obergefell v. Hodges on 26 June 2015; the Montana Supreme Court recognised a common-law same-sex marriage as retroactively valid in Adami v. Nelson on 10 December 2019. Montana permits adoption with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption, affirmed 6-1 in Kulstad v. Maniaci on 7 October 2009, which granted parental rights and set precedent for stepparent adoptions by same-sex couples.
tangentialFactors:
Montana's trajectory runs against the national direction recorded in the July 2026 assessment, where federal policy shifts and litigation keep the youth-side picture unstable and other states' standings declined; Montana is the single exception, improving because its courts have blocked the enacted restrictions rather than because the legislature repealed them.

Official hostility has also been expressed through speech and display rules. House Bill 819, debated 6 March 2025 and signed by Governor Gianforte in May 2025 with immediate effect, prohibits flags representing political party, race, sexual orientation, gender or political ideology on government property and in public schools, thereby banning Pride and other LGBTQ flags, while permitting official historical flags including the Gadsden flag, law-enforcement and Thin Blue Line flags, tribal nation, foreign country, military service branch, POW/MIA and official school or government entity flags.

House Bill 359 of May 2023 prohibited sexually oriented or obscene performances in public spaces where minors may be present and explicitly barred drag story hours at publicly funded schools and libraries; a Butte-Silver Bow library cancelled a transgender woman's reading in response. District Judge Brian Morris issued a temporary restraining order in July 2023, extended in October 2024, blocking enforcement as vague and overbroad with a risk of disproportionate enforcement against trans, Two-Spirit and gender-nonconforming people. A March 2025 bill defining drag as inherently sexual was defeated with 13 Republicans joining Democrats.
localsOnly:
State employment protection has a longer history than statute: personnel rules of 2000 under Governor Marc Racicot barred sexual-orientation discrimination, Executive Order 41-2008 of November 2008 under Governor Brian Schweitzer broadened them, and a January 2016 order under Governor Steve Bullock extended coverage to gender identity and to contractors. Sexual-orientation discrimination is likewise barred in state employment and by contractors by executive order, and by the ordinances of Bozeman, Butte-Silver Bow County, Helena, Missoula and Whitefish in employment, housing and public accommodations. State statutes do not directly address sexual-orientation discrimination.

Montana hate-crime statutes do not cover sexual orientation either, leaving prosecution to federal courts under the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd, Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act of October 2009.

The rules for changing sex markers on resident documents have moved repeatedly. Until December 2017 the state required sex reassignment surgery and clinical treatment, after which the surgery requirement was replaced by a Correction Affidavit, Gender Designation Form, court order and doctor's letter for licences. An April 2021 law reintroducing surgical procedures and a court order was signed effective immediately by Governor Gianforte and blocked in April 2022 for lack of clear legal definitions; the department then imposed a temporary emergency rule in May 2022 banning updates, made permanent months later. That rule and the associated Motor Vehicle Division policy are the measures enjoined in December 2024 and upheld on appeal in April 2026, so marker changes remain unavailable pending trial.

Montana permits adoption by individuals with no explicit prohibitions on same-sex couples or second-parent adoption; lesbian couples have access to in vitro fertilisation with the non-genetic, non-gestational mother recognised if married, and surrogacy is unregulated, with courts generally favourable to pre-birth parentage orders for genetic relationship and case-by-case orders without a genetic link.

House Bill 819 of May 2025 bars official display of flags representing sexual orientation, interpreted as prohibiting Pride flags; Missoula adopted a rainbow pride flag as its municipal flag, a step treated as a loophole effectively exempting it statewide. A May 2021 parental opt-in law requires parental consent before K-12 sex education.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the April 2026 challenge to Senate Bill 437 is unresolved in the sources: plaintiffs moved to add it to the existing litigation as identical to SB 458, and no ruling on that motion is documented.

Whether the April 2025 temporary restraint against House Bill 121 has since been converted into a permanent injunction, or the law allowed to take effect, is not sourced; the same applies to the status of the December 2024 preliminary block on identity-document changes beyond the April 2026 appellate affirmance.

No Montana-specific incidents of violence against trans people, and no state-level count or rate, appear in the inventory, so no assessment of physical risk in the state can be made from these sources. Federal document, entry-screening, custody and care-funding rules are carried by the national record and are not restated here.
